property_summary: For every caller, the stored owner never changes after construction, so c.owner() must always equal the contract deployer regardless of who calls it; the buggy version instead returns the caller's address, so a call from any address other than the deployer yields a different value.
owner() must return the same fixed owner address regardless of which address calls it; the mutant returns the caller's address, so two calls from different addresses yield different values.
After ownership is transferred to any address X, owner() must return X when queried from any other address Y; the mutant returns the querying caller Y instead, so for Y != X the rule is violated.
After renouncing ownership, owner() must return address(0) no matter who queries it; the mutant returns the caller's address, which is nonzero for any caller, violating the rule.

Only the address set via transferOwnership may exercise owner-only functions: after transferring ownership to X, a call to renounceOwnership() from any other address Y must revert in the reference C, while the mutant's owner() returns the caller, so Y is treated as owner and the call succeeds.

For any caller, C's owner() getter always returns the non-zero address that was set at construction (the deployer), never the zero address; the mutant makes owner() return address(0), violating this for every input.

For any admissible address a != address(0), after the current owner calls transferOwnership(a), a subsequent call to owner() must complete and return exactly a; the mutant's owner() always returns address(0), so the ownership check inside transferOwnership fails and the call reverts for every a.

For any caller, if renounceOwnership() completes it must set the owner to the zero address, and the deploying owner must always be able to renounce; the mutant's owner() returning address(0) makes _checkOwner fail, so the owner's renounce reverts and owner() stays non-zero.

For any non-zero address a, a call to setCaller(a) issued by the deploying owner must complete without reverting (onlyOwner check passes); the mutant's owner() always returns address(0), so the owner's own setCaller reverts for every input.

For any non-owner caller a, c.renounceOwnership() must revert (Ownable's _checkOwner rejects callers unequal to owner()); the mutant's owner() returning address(0) lets address(0) pass the check, so renouncing succeeds and the revert-bool invariant breaks for a == address(0).

For any caller, C.owner() must return the deployer's address stored in the Ownable contract; the mutant's owner() has no return statement so it returns address(0), violating this rule for every input.

For any nonzero fuzzed address, the deployer (this test contract, the stored owner) can successfully execute the onlyOwner function setCaller(actor); the mutant's owner() returns address(0), so _checkOwner fails and every such call reverts, breaking the rule.

For any nonzero address newOwner, transferring ownership from the current owner must make c.owner() equal newOwner; the mutant's owner() returns address(0), so transferOwnership reverts (ownership can never be changed) and the rule fails.

For any fuzzed address a, the onlyOwner entry setCaller(a) succeeds exactly when invoked by the contract's owner (the deployer) and reverts otherwise; the mutant's owner() returns address(0), so _checkOwner rejects even the real owner and the call reverts for the input a == deployer.

For any admissible non-zero address a and cfg v>0, the owner can delegate authority via setCaller(a), after which a can successfully execute setCfg(v) and the public deadCfg getter equals v; the mutant's owner() returns address(0), so _checkOwner rejects the real owner in setCaller, the delegation chain breaks, and a's setCfg(v) call reverts.
